items.headline: Radiation Oncology Takes Center Stage as Mayo Clinic Unveils Research at ASTRO 2026
items.preview: Mayo Clinic researchers are set to present groundbreaking findings at the ASTRO 2026 Annual Meeting.
items.article:
Boston is about to become the epicenter of radiation medicine as the 2026 American Society for Radiation Oncology Annual Meeting convenes from September 26 through 30. Mayo Clinic researchers will participate in nearly 65 sessions and deliver 45 abstracts covering topics such as artificial intelligence, precision treatment outcomes, and novel radiotherapy techniques.
Why this matters: The presentations could reshape standards of care for challenging cancers in both adults and children, highlighting advancements in radiation oncology and the integration of AI in treatment planning and delivery.
Key contributions include results from a trial on metastatic Ewing sarcoma, showcasing the highest event-free survival recorded in cooperative-group trials, and discussions on AI-driven automation in pelvic radiation therapy, which may lead to more personalized treatment approaches.

items.headline: Oral Wnt-blocking pill plus lenvatinib shows promise in endometrial cancer after immunotherapy fails
items.preview: A new oral drug, E7386, combined with lenvatinib shows significant potential for treating advanced endometrial cancer.
items.article:
An experimental oral cancer drug, E7386, has demonstrated durable tumor shrinkage in women with advanced endometrial cancer who had previously failed chemotherapy and immunotherapy. This finding, from a phase 1b/2 trial, suggests a new treatment avenue for patients with limited options.
Why this matters: The combination of E7386 with lenvatinib resulted in a 36.7% objective response rate, significantly higher than conventional second-line chemotherapy, indicating a potential breakthrough in treating this aggressive cancer.
The study included 30 women and showed promising results, with a median progression-free survival of 5.5 months and a disease control rate of 70%. Safety data indicated manageable side effects, paving the way for further exploration of this combination therapy.

items.headline: This week in charts: Novo’s rise and fall and AI biotechs’ big haul
items.preview: Novo's stock has plummeted while AI drug discovery startups secure significant funding.
items.article:
Novo's share price has dramatically fallen from record highs due to increased competition and disappointing clinical results. Following a recent capital markets day, shares dropped further, indicating investor skepticism about the company's future.
Why this matters: The decline in Novo's stock reflects broader challenges in the biotech sector, while AI drug discovery startups are thriving, securing large funding rounds and demonstrating the growing interest in AI applications in medicine.
This week, notable funding successes included Enveda, which raised $311 million, and Basecamp Research, which secured $140 million, highlighting the shift towards AI-driven drug development amidst traditional biotech struggles.

items.headline: Novo pursues long-acting obesity drugs; Acadia slumps on Alzheimer’s data
items.preview: Novo partners with Nanexa for long-acting drug delivery technology amid Acadia's trial setbacks.
items.article:
Novo has entered a partnership with Nanexa to develop long-acting injectable medicines for obesity and Type 2 diabetes, investing up to $1.32 billion in the technology. This move aims to enhance treatment options with less frequent dosing schedules.
Why this matters: As Novo seeks to innovate in the obesity market, Acadia Pharmaceuticals faces challenges with its Alzheimer’s drug, which narrowly missed efficacy in trials. Despite this, Acadia continues its Phase 3 studies, indicating a commitment to finding effective treatments.
In other news, the FDA approved a new weekly insulin from Eli Lilly, and Merck expanded the use of its kidney cancer drug Welireg, reflecting ongoing advancements in diabetes and cancer treatments.

items.headline: How reverse merger-plus-PIPE deals came to rival the IPO path to market
items.preview: Reverse mergers are becoming a viable alternative for biotech companies seeking public listings.
items.article:
Reverse mergers, once viewed as a less prestigious route to going public, are gaining traction among biotech firms. This shift is attributed to the availability of shell companies and investor interest in concurrent PIPEs, making it a more attractive option.
Why this matters: The evolving perception of reverse mergers reflects changing dynamics in the biotech financing landscape, offering companies a faster and potentially less costly path to market compared to traditional IPOs.
As more biotechs explore this route, it may reshape how companies approach public listings and funding strategies in the future.
